content.text:
Yes—but with a caveat: **most “new” literary genres are not wholly new from nothing**. They usually crystallize older themes, media, and readerships into a recognizable label. In the 21st century, several genres/subgenres have either emerged or become newly codified:

- **Cli-fi / climate fiction**: Fiction centered on climate change and ecological crisis. Climate-themed writing predates this century, but “cli-fi” became a recognizable label in the 2000s–2010s, with the term often credited to Dan Bloom around 2007–2008. ([merriam-webster.com](https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/cli-fi-clifi-climate-fiction-genre-words-were-watching?utm_source=openai))

- **LitRPG / GameLit**: Novels that incorporate role-playing-game mechanics—levels, stats, quests, skill trees—into the narrative itself. The label **LitRPG** is usually traced to the early 2010s, especially Russian publishing circles, and has since grown through web fiction, Kindle, audiobooks, and fan communities. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LitRPG?utm_source=openai))

- **New Adult fiction**: A market category between YA and adult fiction, typically focused on protagonists aged about 18–29 dealing with college, first jobs, sex, independence, and identity. The term was coined by St. Martin’s Press in 2009. ([ebsco.com](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/literature-and-writing/new-adult-fiction?utm_source=openai))

- **Solarpunk**: A hopeful speculative-fiction mode imagining sustainable, ecological, post-carbon futures. It overlaps with sci-fi, utopian fiction, and environmental literature, but the term **solarpunk** was coined in 2008 and became a recognizable aesthetic/literary movement online. ([builtin.com](https://builtin.com/articles/solarpunk?utm_source=openai))

- **Cell-phone novels / mobile fiction**: Serialized fiction written for and often on mobile phones, especially prominent in Japan in the early 2000s. The form shaped pacing, sentence length, serialization, and intimacy of address in ways tied to mobile reading culture. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_phone_novel?utm_source=openai))

- **Creepypasta / internet horror**: Horror circulated through forums, wikis, social media, and copy-paste culture. It descends from urban legend and Gothic/horror fiction, but its networked authorship, anonymity, remixing, and viral spread are distinctively 21st-century.

- **Twitterature, Instapoetry, and platform-native micro-literature**: Very short literary forms shaped by social platforms—character limits, feeds, screenshots, hashtags, visual layout, and shareability. They are related to aphorism, haiku, epigram, and concrete poetry, but their distribution and audience formation are new.

- **Born-digital / electronic literature**: Interactive fiction, hypertext, generative poetry, VR narratives, AI-assisted narratives, and multimedia works where the “text” depends on code, links, interface, or user interaction. Electronic literature began in the late 20th century, but it expanded dramatically in the 21st century as a family of genres. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/nature-index/topics/l3/digital-literature?utm_source=openai))

So the short answer is: **yes, but many are better understood as new labels, markets, media forms, or subgenres rather than brand-new genres in the old sense**. The biggest genuinely 21st-century changes come from **climate consciousness**, **gaming culture**, and **digital platforms**.
